working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: Rather than declaring a winner, this post works through the real decision criteria UK club golfers face (course terrain, boot space, budget, playing frequency) to help them land on the right type of trolley for their specific situation. It treats the question as genuinely open and avoids defaulting to 'just spend more'.
research_notes:
- Two dominant market segments: push (manual 3-wheel) and electric (handle-controlled, remote, follow). Two-wheel pull trolleys are a distant third and generally considered poor for the body owing to the twisting motion on one side.
- Push trolleys beat electric on storage space as standard, lighter overall weight, simpler transport/storage, and no charging requirement. Better fit for flatter courses and occasional golfers.
- Electric trolleys conserve energy across a full round because the motor does the work. Particularly valuable on hilly UK courses, in wet/soft conditions, and for golfers with back or joint concerns.
- Key electric sub-types to explain: handle-controlled (manual steering), remote-controlled, follow/auto. Follow trolleys typically cost the most.
- Electric downhill braking (e.g. Motocaddy DHC, electronic braking systems) is a genuine safety and convenience feature on steep UK parkland — worth flagging.
- Battery types: lithium vs older lead-acid. Lithium is lighter, charges faster, more reliable. Battery size (18-hole, 27-hole, 36-hole) should be matched to how hilly the course is and whether multiple rounds are played.
- Compact fold matters more on electric trolleys because the battery adds weight — a poor fold is a practical daily frustration.
- Boot space is a real-world UK constraint: measure car boot before buying, especially for electric models.
- Key UK brands: PowaKaddy (FX, CT, Micra ranges) and Motocaddy (M-series, S-series, Cube Push) lead the market. Stewart Golf, Clicgear, Big Max, Bag Boy, Sun Mountain also notable.
- Rough price ranges visible in current retailer listings (2026): quality push trolleys from roughly £150–£220; entry electric from roughly £550; mid-range GPS electric from roughly £800–£1,100+. (These are indicative only — do not present as definitive in post; advise readers to check current retailer pricing.)
- Winter wheels / all-terrain wheels worth mentioning for year-round UK use.
- A trolley and bag must be compatible — worth a brief mention (especially PowaKaddy MAG-LOK system works best with PowaKaddy bags).
must_avoid:
- No fabricated prices or specs beyond the indicative ranges noted above; direct readers to check current retailer pricing rather than stating definitive figures.
- No invented quotes attributed to reviewers, pros, or brand reps.
- No affiliate links to trolley products unless they appear in approved-partners.md; mention brands and models informationally only if not approved.
- No health/medical advice beyond generic framing (e.g. 'easier on the body' is fine; specific claims about injury prevention or rehabilitation are not).
- No financial advice on whether a golfer can or should afford an electric trolley — describe costs factually and neutrally.
- No personal anecdote implying the site owner has tested specific trolleys unless supplied in the brief.
- No em dashes anywhere in the post.
- This is a Gear post, not a Travel/Courses post — keep focus on the equipment decision, not specific course recommendations.
